period: Old Kingdom to Roman; most standing temples are New Kingdom or Ptolemaic
summary: An Egyptian temple was not a church for worshippers but a house for a god, built as a model of the first morning of creation.
look: You will walk this plan again and again: Philae in Aswan, Kom Ombo and Edfu on the 20th, Karnak and Luxor on the 22nd. Find the main axis and follow it from the pylon gateway, through the open court and the column hall, to the small dark sanctuary at the back. Notice the floor rising and the roof dropping as you go in. Somewhere in the enclosure there is usually a sacred lake, and often a stone stand for the god's boat.
story:
The Egyptians called a temple hwt-netjer, the mansion of the god, and they meant it literally. The god lived in the sanctuary as a statue inside a stone or wooden shrine, the naos. Ordinary people stayed outside: they prayed at the gates, left offerings in outer chapels and met the god only when he came out in procession. The point of the whole operation was maat, the order of the universe. Keep the god fed and content and the sun rises, the Nile floods and chaos stays out. In theory the king was the only priest, which is why he performs every ritual on the walls; in practice priests stood in for him.

The building is a model of creation. The pylon is the horizon, two hills with the sun rising between them, with grooves for tall flagpoles. The open court leads into the hypostyle hall, a papyrus marsh in stone. Then the floor climbs and the roof drops toward the sanctuary, the mound that first rose from the waters of chaos. Each dawn a priest broke the clay seal on the shrine, woke the god, washed, anointed, dressed and fed the statue, then sealed it again. The food then went to the priests.

Temples were also economic giants, with farms, herds, workshops and ships, employing tens of thousands. On the West Bank, 'mansions of millions of years' served the dead king and Amun together; many Egyptologists now doubt there was a sharp line between cult temples and mortuary temples. The last temples closed between the 4th and 6th centuries AD.
details: Pylon front: look for the tall vertical grooves where cedar flagpoles stood, and the king smiting enemies on each tower.
Karnak's Hypostyle: open papyrus-flower capitals on the tall central aisle, closed-bud capitals on the lower side aisles.
Raised relief inside, sunk relief outside, where hard sunlight throws the carving into shadow. Compare an outer and an inner wall.
Look up under roofs and architraves for surviving paint: blues, greens and reds last where sun and rain never reached.
A full temple kit: enclosure wall, sacred lake (Karnak), birth house or mammisi (Edfu, Philae), storerooms and priests' houses.
fun_fact: Herodotus says Egyptian priests shaved their whole bodies every other day and wore only linen and papyrus sandals; wool was not allowed into temples.
narration: You are standing in a house, not a church. The Egyptians called a temple the mansion of the god, and the god really lived here, as a statue in a stone shrine in the darkest room at the back. Ordinary people stayed outside the gates. Inside, priests acted for the king, who in theory performed every ritual himself. That is why, on almost every wall, you see the pharaoh offering bread, wine or a tiny figure of the goddess Maat to a god. The whole building is a model of the first morning of the world. The great gateway, the pylon, stands for the horizon, two hills with the sun rising between them. The forest of columns is a papyrus marsh turned to stone. Walk on and the floor rises while the roof drops, until you reach the sanctuary, the mound that first rose out of the waters of chaos. Every dawn a priest broke the clay seal on the shrine doors, woke the god, washed him, dressed him in fresh linen and served him breakfast. Once the god had eaten in spirit, the priests ate the food. Temples were also landlords, with fields, herds, ships and thousands of workers. Now look along the main axis toward the back: that narrowing line of doorways is the path the god's boat took on festival days.

summary: A royal tomb is a guidebook to the underworld, painted so the dead king could ride with the sun through twelve hours of night and rise again.
look: You meet these books in the Valley of the Kings on the 21st. The corridors slope down into the mountain like the sun sinking in the west, and the burial chamber is the deepest room. Look for long horizontal bands of figures separated by columns of text, a ram-headed god in a boat, and huge snakes. A dark blue ceiling with yellow stars, or a long arched goddess, means you have reached the sky books.
story:
Royal funerary texts grew over 1,500 years. The Pyramid Texts, carved inside Unas' pyramid around 2400 BC, helped the king climb to the sky. The Coffin Texts of the Middle Kingdom spread spells to wealthy officials. In the New Kingdom, kings had their own 'books of the netherworld', and the tomb itself became a model of the sun's night journey.

The oldest is the Amduat, 'what is in the underworld'. Fragments appear in tombs of Thutmose I and Hatshepsut, but the first complete copy is in KV34, Thutmose III's tomb. It splits the night into 12 hours, in three bands, with the sun god sailing his boat along the middle band. He has a ram's head: the ram was written with the same sign as ba, the soul. In the 5th hour the boat crosses the sandy realm of Sokar; in the 7th the serpent Apophis is fettered and cut; in the 12th the sun is reborn as the scarab Khepri.

Later books add variety. The Litany of Ra, near tomb entrances, lists 75 forms of the sun. The Book of Gates has 12 gates guarded by serpents, the hall of Osiris' judgement and the four peoples of humankind. The Book of Caverns punishes the sun's enemies. After Amarna, the Books of the Sky put Nut on the ceiling, swallowing the sun at dusk and giving birth to it at dawn; from Ramesses IV two were often painted side by side.

The aim of it all: the king unites with Ra, who travels, and with Osiris, who rests, and rises with the sun every morning.
details: KV34, Thutmose III: the Amduat painted like an unrolled papyrus, with stick-like figures on a beige background.
KV9, Ramesses V and VI: two long Nut figures stretch back to back across the burial chamber ceiling.
KV17, Seti I: the first tomb decorated in every corridor and chamber, with the Litany of Ra near the entrance.
Find the sun god as a ram-headed man standing in a shrine on his boat, often wrapped in the coils of the Mehen serpent.
Upside-down or headless figures in a lower band are the sun's enemies, punished in the Book of Caverns.
fun_fact: The burial chamber of KV34 has rounded corners, shaped like a giant cartouche, so Thutmose III was laid to rest inside his own name.
narration: Think of every royal tomb in the Valley as a map of one night. The Egyptians watched the sun die in the west each evening and come back in the east each morning, and they wanted their king to make the same trip. So the corridors slope down into the mountain like a sunset, and the walls carry guidebooks to the underworld. The oldest is the Amduat, which means what is in the underworld. It splits the night into 12 hours. The sun god sails through them in a boat, with the head of a ram, because the sign for ram also wrote the word for soul. Around the 7th hour the giant serpent Apophis tries to stop the boat and is tied up and cut. In the last hour the sun is reborn as a scarab beetle and rolls out into the dawn. Later kings added more books. The Book of Gates has 12 doors, each guarded by a serpent. The Book of Caverns shows the sun's enemies punished, some of them upside down. On the ceilings you will often find the sky goddess Nut, swallowing the sun at dusk and giving birth to it at dawn. The king joins both great gods: he rides with Ra, and he rests as Osiris. Here is the 2-minute trick for any tomb. Near the door, the king greets the falcon-headed sun. Down the corridors, the night journey. In the deepest room, rebirth. Now find the sun's boat on the wall and see which way it is sailing.

period: New Kingdom to Ptolemaic, c. 1550-50 BC
summary: Not a bible but a pick-and-mix of about 190 spells, bought by anyone who could afford one, to get the dead through the gods' final exam.
look: You will see its pictures on papyri and coffins at the GEM, and painted on tomb walls at Deir el-Medina and in Nefertari's tomb on the 21st. The famous scene is the weighing: a big balance, a heart on one pan, a feather on the other, a jackal-headed god at the scales and a crocodile-headed monster sitting by. Read it like a comic strip: the dead person led in, judged, then presented to Osiris on his throne.
story:
The Egyptian title was 'Spells for Going Forth by Day'; the name Book of the Dead comes from the German Todtenbuch, coined by Karl Richard Lepsius in 1842. It was never a fixed book. About 192 spells are known, but no papyrus contains them all: buyers chose a selection, and cheaper scrolls came ready-made with a gap for the owner's name. The tradition grew out of the royal Pyramid Texts and the Middle Kingdom Coffin Texts, appeared at Thebes around 1700 BC and was used until about 50 BC. Only in the 26th Dynasty did priests put the spells in a standard order.

Spell 125 is the judgement, first known from the time of Hatshepsut and Thutmose III. In the Hall of Two Truths the dead address 42 judges, each by name, and deny a list of wrongs: theft, murder, cheating with the scales, making others weep. Then Anubis weighs the heart, seat of memory and conscience, against the feather of Maat. Thoth records the verdict. Ammit, 'devourer of the dead', waits to swallow a heart heavy with wrongdoing: a second death with no return. The justified are led by Horus to Osiris.

Other spells keep the person together. Spell 25 helps you remember your own name, spells 26 to 30 protect the heart and were carved on heart scarabs, and spell 6 wakes the shabtis. The goal was the Field of Reeds, an idealised Egypt of endless harvests. The finest surviving copy, the Papyrus of Ani, was bought at Luxor by Wallis Budge in 1888 and is in the British Museum.
details: The weighing: Anubis checks the balance, Thoth stands by with his scribe's palette, Ammit waits, and the dead person watches.
Along the top of many judgement scenes runs a row of small seated figures: the 42 judges of the Hall of Two Truths.
A human-headed bird near the dead person is the ba, the part of the soul that could fly out of the tomb by day.
Sennedjem's tomb, TT1 at Deir el-Medina (21st): the Field of Reeds, with the couple ploughing and reaping beside canals.
In museum cases, heart scarabs are large, flat-bottomed and often of dark stone, with the heart spell carved underneath.
fun_fact: The heart-scarab spell came with a pedigree: its label claims Prince Hordjedef, a son of Khufu, found it in Menkaure's reign, centuries before any surviving copy.
narration: That big balance you keep seeing is the most famous scene in Egyptian religion: the weighing of the heart. It comes from the Book of the Dead, which was never really one book. The Egyptians called it the Spells for Going Forth by Day, and about 190 spells are known. Families bought a scroll with a selection, sometimes ready-made, with a gap left for the name. Spell 125 is the final exam. The dead person walks into the Hall of Two Truths and faces 42 judges, denying a list of sins: I have not stolen, I have not killed, I have not made anyone weep. Then comes the test. Anubis, the jackal god, puts the heart on one pan of the scales and the feather of Maat, truth, on the other. The heart held memory and conscience, so it could tell tales. That is why a heart scarab on the mummy's chest carried a spell begging the heart not to testify against its owner. Thoth, the ibis-headed scribe, writes down the verdict. Beside the scales crouches Ammit, the devourer, with the head of a crocodile, the front of a lion and the rear of a hippo. If the heart is heavy, she eats it, and that is the second, final death. If it balances, Horus leads the dead to Osiris, and on to the Field of Reeds, a perfect Egypt with endless harvests. In the next judgement scene you find, look at the scales: a pointer standing exactly upright means justified.

period: c. 3600 BC to the Roman period
summary: The body was the soul's home address: embalmers spent 70 days drying, filling and wrapping it so the spirit could find its way back.
look: You meet mummies three ways on this trip: Tutankhamun himself, still in his tomb, on the 21st; the small Mummification Museum on the Luxor corniche on the 22nd; and the royal mummies at NMEC in Cairo if you get there. Look for the embalming cut on the left side of the belly, the linen wrappings and amulets, and the jars and tools that came out of and went into the body.
story:
For an Egyptian, a person was made of several parts: the body, the name, the shadow, the heart, the ka or life force, and the ba, a human-headed bird that left the tomb by day. Kept together and fed, they let the dead become an akh, a transfigured spirit. The ba needed a recognisable body to return to; the ka could also live in a statue, a spare body in stone.

The earliest Egyptians were preserved by accident, dried in hot sand, but by about 3600 BC some were already wrapped in linen with resin and plant oils. True evisceration began around the 4th Dynasty, and the classic method peaked in the New Kingdom. The brain was broken up with a rod pushed through the nose and drained; Herodotus thought an iron hook pulled it out. A cut in the left flank removed the liver, lungs, stomach and intestines, which were dried and placed in four canopic jars. The heart, seat of thought, stayed inside. The body was covered in natron, a natural salt, for about 40 days, then oiled, resined and wrapped in linen with amulets; the whole job took 70 days. Priests then performed the Opening of the Mouth so the mummy could breathe, eat and speak.

Herodotus also lists cheaper options, such as cedar oil injected to dissolve the organs. Over a million animal mummies have been found, many of them cats and ibises. Europeans later ground mummies into medicine and paint pigment, and Victorians unwrapped them for entertainment. In 1903 Thutmose IV became the first mummy to be X-rayed.
details: Embalming cut: on the left side of the abdomen, sometimes covered by a small plate decorated with the Eye of Horus.
Crossed arms on the chest mark many New Kingdom kings; most other mummies lie with arms straight at the sides.
Mummification Museum, Luxor (22nd): natron, resins, embalming tools and animal mummies, from a cat to a crocodile.
Tutankhamun's own mummy still lies in his tomb, KV62, in a glass case: you can see his face on the 21st.
In later mummies, linen, sawdust or mud was packed under the skin to restore a lifelike shape.
fun_fact: For centuries Europeans swallowed powdered mummy as medicine; in 1599 the English writer Richard Hakluyt grumbled that apothecaries made people take it against their will.
narration: Why go to all this trouble? Because for an Egyptian, death split a person into pieces. There was the body, the name and the shadow. There was the ka, the life force, which stayed in the tomb and needed feeding. And there was the ba, a bird with a human head, which flew out by day and had to find its body again at night. If the body rotted, the ba was homeless. So the embalmers worked for 70 days. First they broke up the brain with a rod pushed through the nose and let it drain out. Herodotus thought they pulled it out with an iron hook, but experiments show liquefying works far better. They threw the brain away. Then they cut the left side of the belly and removed the liver, lungs, stomach and intestines, each dried and stored in its own jar. The heart stayed in, because it held your mind and would be weighed at the judgement. The body was packed and covered with natron, a natural salt from desert lakes, for about 40 days, until it was dry as leather. Then came oils, resin and many layers of linen, with protective amulets tucked between the wrappings. The Egyptians mummified animals too, more than a million of them, many cats and ibises. Europeans later ground mummies into medicine. Next time you see a mummy, look at the left side of the belly for the embalmer's cut, often hidden under a small plate.

summary: A field guide to tomb equipment: the jars for the organs, the little workers who answered for you, and the door only spirits could use.
look: These fill museum cases at the GEM and turn up in every tomb you visit. Four lidded jars in a set are canopic jars; rows of small mummy-shaped figures holding hoes are shabtis; a flat stone slab carved like a recessed doorway, usually on a west wall, is a false door. Read the text on any of them for the name of the owner.
story:
Canopic jars held the organs removed during mummification. The name is a mistake by early scholars, who linked them to Canopus, helmsman of Menelaus, worshipped in the Delta in the form of a jar. Old Kingdom jars had plain lids; human heads became common later; by the 19th Dynasty the four lids were the sons of Horus. In later periods the organs were wrapped and put back in the body, and dummy jars were buried for form's sake.

Shabtis, later called ushabtis, were servant figures. Their spell, Coffin Text 472 and later Book of the Dead spell 6, promises that if the owner is called to plough, fill the canals or carry sand in the next world, the figure will step up and say 'here I am'. From the 21st Dynasty tombs could hold hundreds, with an overseer holding a whip for every gang of ten; the Kushite king Taharqa had more than a thousand.

The false door, standard in Old Kingdom tombs and usually on the west wall, was the threshold where the ka came out to eat. Before it lay an offering slab, and around it ran the offering formula, hetep-di-nesu, 'an offering which the king gives', asking for a thousand of bread, beer, oxen and fowl for the owner's ka.
details: Canopic lids: human Imsety (liver), baboon Hapy (lungs), jackal Duamutef (stomach), falcon Qebehsenuef (intestines).
Tutankhamun's canopic stoppers show his own face, not animal heads: compare them with later sets.
Shabtis: read down the legs; the spell begins with the owner's name, styled 'the Osiris' plus the name.
Overseer shabtis wear a kilt and hold a whip; there was roughly one for every ten workers.
Offering formula on stelae: look for a sedge plant, a loaf on a mat and a pointed loaf, read hetep-di-nesu.
fun_fact: Tutankhamun took 413 shabtis with him; one popular theory says that is a worker for each day of the year plus overseers to keep them at it.
narration: Here is a quick field guide to the things you will see in every tomb case. First, canopic jars, always in sets of 4. They held the liver, lungs, stomach and intestines. The name is a Greek mix-up: early scholars linked them to Canopus, the helmsman of Menelaus, said to be worshipped in the Delta in the form of a jar. From the late New Kingdom the lids show the 4 sons of Horus: a man for the liver, a baboon for the lungs, a jackal for the stomach and a falcon for the intestines. Next, the shabtis, little mummy-shaped figures with hoes. Their spell says that if the dead are called up for farm work in the next world, the shabti will answer: here I am, I will do it. Some people had hundreds, with overseer figures holding whips. Last, the false door: a carved doorway that does not open, usually on the west wall. The spirit stepped through it to eat the food left on the slab in front. Look for the first signs of the offering prayer: a sedge plant, a loaf on a mat and a pointed loaf, meaning an offering which the king gives.

summary: Grandfather, son and grandson built the three Giza pyramids within about a century, yet we barely know them as people.
look: You meet them at the GEM on the 11th and on the Giza plateau on the 12th. The biggest pyramid is Khufu's; the one with a cap of smooth casing near its tip is Khafre's, and it looks tallest only because it stands on higher ground; the smallest is Menkaure's. In the museums, look for Khafre enthroned with a falcon behind his head, Menkaure's triads with Hathor, and Khufu's tiny ivory statuette.
story:
Sneferu, almost certainly Khufu's father, built three pyramids at Meidum and Dahshur and turned the stepped shape into a true pyramid by trial and error. Khufu, short for Khnum-khufu, 'Khnum protects me', reigned in the 26th century BC for at least 27 years. Papyri found in 2013 at the Red Sea harbour of Wadi al-Jarf include the logbook of an inspector called Merer, who shipped limestone from Tura to Giza late in Khufu's reign. The king's only complete statue is an ivory figurine found by Flinders Petrie at Abydos in 1903; its head turned up after three weeks of sieving.

Khufu's son Djedefre reigned briefly and built at Abu Rawash. Another son, Khafre, built the second Giza pyramid, 'Khafre is great', and most Egyptologists credit him with the Sphinx. More statues survive of Khafre than of any other Old Kingdom king; Auguste Mariette found several in a pit in his valley temple in 1860. His son Menkaure built the smallest of the three, about 103 metres a side and 65 high, but left the finest sculpture: greywacke triads of the king with Hathor and province gods, and a pair statue with his queen. After him, Shepseskaf chose a mastaba tomb, and Giza's great age was over.

Herodotus, writing some 2,000 years later, portrayed Khufu and Khafre as tyrants who closed the temples and Menkaure as pious. That reflects later legend, not the evidence: Khufu's memory was honoured for centuries, and later storytellers set the magicians' tales of the Westcar Papyrus at his court.
details: Khafre's pyramid keeps a cap of its smooth white casing near the top: once, all three pyramids looked like that.
Menkaure's pyramid: the vertical gash in the north face comes from a failed attempt to demolish it in 1196.
Khafre's diorite statue: Horus the falcon spreads his wings behind the king's head. Find it in the museum.
Menkaure triads: the king between Hathor and a province goddess, who wears her province's emblem on her head.
Khufu's dismantled cedar boats were buried beside his pyramid; the first one is rebuilt at the GEM.
fun_fact: Menkaure's stone sarcophagus survived over 4,000 years inside his pyramid, then sank with the ship carrying it to England in 1838.
narration: Three kings, three generations, one plateau. Khufu came first, in the 26th century BC. His full name was Khnum-khufu, Khnum protects me. His father, almost certainly Sneferu, had built 3 pyramids and found the true pyramid shape by trial and error. Khufu took the lesson and built the biggest of all. Strangely, the only complete statue of him is an ivory figurine smaller than your hand. Flinders Petrie found it headless in 1903, stopped all work and had his men sieve the rubble for 3 weeks until the head turned up. After Khufu came one son, Djedefre, then another, Khafre, who built the second pyramid and, most Egyptologists think, the Sphinx. More statues survive of Khafre than of any other Old Kingdom king. His son Menkaure built the smallest of the three pyramids but left the finest sculpture: the king striding beside the goddess Hathor. 2,000 years later, Herodotus heard that Khufu and Khafre were cruel tyrants and Menkaure was kind. That is later legend, not history. A far better witness has survived: the logbook of Merer, an inspector who shipped limestone blocks along the Nile to Khufu's building site. When you look at the three pyramids, remember that the middle one only looks tallest because it stands on higher rock.

summary: A king's daughter and king's wife who made herself king, ruled about 20 prosperous years, and was then chiselled out of history.
look: Her thread runs through the trip: the Unfinished Obelisk in Aswan, her terraced temple at Deir el-Bahari on the 21st, her obelisk and Red Chapel at Karnak on the 22nd. Recognise her by the throne name Maatkare in a cartouche, and by statues of a bearded, kilted king whose inscriptions slip into feminine grammar. Many of her figures and names were hacked out, so a neat chiselled hollow in a relief is often her.
story:
Hatshepsut was the eldest daughter of Thutmose I and Queen Ahmose. She married her half-brother Thutmose II and had a daughter, Neferure. When he died, the heir was Thutmose III, son of a minor wife, still a small child. Hatshepsut acted as regent, and by his year 7 she was king, sharing his count of years but as the senior partner. Her official images gradually lost their femininity: the khat headcloth, uraeus, false beard and kilt. Her temple's divine birth reliefs explain that Amun visited her mother in the guise of Thutmose I and Khnum shaped the child on his wheel.

Her reign, about 1479 to 1458 BC counting the regency, was prosperous and mostly peaceful. In year 9 her ships reached Punt and returned with 31 live myrrh trees. She raised two great obelisks at Karnak, one still standing; the cracked Unfinished Obelisk at Aswan is often linked to her. She built the Red Chapel at Karnak and Djeser-Djeseru, 'holiest of holies', at Deir el-Bahari, helped by officials such as her steward Senenmut.

She vanishes from the record around year 22 of Thutmose III. Late in his reign and under Amenhotep II, her statues were smashed and her name erased. Because this began some 20 years after her death, most scholars see it as securing his son's succession rather than personal revenge. In 2007 a mummy from tomb KV60 was identified as hers by a loose tooth, kept in a box bearing her name, that fitted its jaw. She was overweight and about 50; some experts remain cautious. She is now at NMEC.
details: Her throne name Maatkare: a sun disc, the seated goddess Maat with her feather, and the raised arms of the ka.
Deir el-Bahari (21st): the Punt reliefs on the middle terrace show incense trees carried to the ships in baskets.
Karnak (22nd): her standing obelisk is the second-tallest ancient obelisk still upright; its twin's tip lies by the lake.
Erasures: a neat hollow where a figure was cut out, sometimes recarved as an offering table or another king's name.
Aswan: the Unfinished Obelisk, cracked in the quarry and abandoned, is often linked to her reign.
fun_fact: She is said to have ground charred frankincense from Punt into kohl, so the most powerful person in Egypt wore perfumed eyeliner.
narration: Hatshepsut was the daughter of a king, the wife of a king, and then, unusually, a king herself. Her father was Thutmose the First. She married her half-brother Thutmose the Second, and when he died young, the heir was a small boy, Thutmose the Third, the son of a minor wife. Hatshepsut ruled for him as regent, and within about 7 years she had taken the full titles of a pharaoh. Her official images show a man, with a kilt, a broad chest and a false beard, because that was what a king looked like. Yet the inscriptions often slip into feminine grammar. To justify it all, her temple tells how the god Amun visited her mother disguised as her father, and how Khnum shaped the baby on his potter's wheel. Her reign of about 20 years was peaceful and rich. She sent ships to the land of Punt, which came back with 31 live myrrh trees. She raised giant obelisks at Karnak and built the terraced temple at Deir el-Bahari. Some 20 years after her death, her statues were smashed and her names cut out. Most scholars now think this was cold dynastic politics, not revenge. In 2007 her mummy was identified thanks to a single tooth that fitted a gap in its jaw. It is now at NMEC in Cairo. Next time you see a neat chiselled hollow where a king's figure should be, ask whether it was her.

period: New Kingdom, 18th Dynasty, c. 1479-1425 and c. 1388-1350 BC
summary: One king built Egypt's empire on campaign; his great-grandson spent its profits on the most lavish golden age Egypt ever knew.
look: Thutmose III's throne name Menkheperre, a sun disc, a scarab and a game board, is the most common name on scarabs, so you will see it in every museum and shop. His Festival Hall and war Annals are at Karnak on the 22nd, and his tomb, KV34, is in the Valley on the 21st. Amenhotep III left you the Colossi of Memnon, Luxor Temple's great colonnade and sun court, and lion-headed Sekhmet statues by the hundred.
story:
Thutmose III was the son of Thutmose II by a minor wife, Iset. Crowned as a child in 1479 BC, he spent about 22 years as junior partner to Hatshepsut, by the end commanding her armies. Sole ruler from about 1458, he died in his 54th year, in 1425 BC. His Annals at Karnak record at least 16 campaigns. At Megiddo he overruled his generals and took the narrow Aruna pass, but his troops stopped to plunder and the city held out seven or eight months. In his 33rd year he hauled boats overland from Byblos, crossed the Euphrates and set up a stela beside his grandfather's. Syrian plants and animals he saw are carved in the 'Botanical Garden' at Karnak. James Breasted called him the Napoleon of Egypt; his tomb, KV34, holds the first complete Amduat.

Amenhotep III, his great-grandson, became king between 6 and 12 and ruled about 38 years. He fought one Nubian campaign and otherwise enjoyed peace and imperial income. He married Tiye, daughter of the courtiers Yuya and Thuya, and publicised the marriage, a lake dug for her and his lion hunts on large scarabs. He also took Mitannian and Babylonian princesses as diplomatic wives. He built the Malkata palace, much of Luxor Temple and the largest mortuary temple of all, now reduced to the Colossi of Memnon. He celebrated three Sed festivals, and in his 30th year called himself 'the dazzling sun disc', a hint of the Aten religion his son would impose.
details: Menkheperre, Thutmose III's throne name: sun disc, scarab and game board. It is the commonest name on scarabs.
Karnak Akh-menu (22nd): the 'Botanical Garden' room shows plants and animals from Syria, some of them fanciful.
Karnak: his Annals surround the granite sanctuary; Megiddo is the first and longest campaign told.
Colossi of Memnon (21st): Greek and Latin verses by Roman-era visitors cover the legs of the northern statue.
Luxor Museum (22nd): Thutmose III in greywacke, a young idealised face, and Amenhotep III with Sobek in calcite.
fun_fact: After an earthquake cracked the northern Colossus of Memnon, it 'sang' at dawn, and Greek visitors decided it was the Trojan hero Memnon greeting his mother Eos.
narration: These two kings bookend the high point of Egypt's empire. Thutmose the Third spent his first 20 years in the shadow of his stepmother Hatshepsut. Once he ruled alone, he never stopped marching. On his first campaign, at Megiddo, his generals begged him to take the safe roads round the mountain. He called them cowards and led the army single file through a narrow pass, horse after horse and man after man, and came out behind the enemy. Then his soldiers stopped to loot the camp, and he had to besiege the city for 7 months. Later he carried boats overland to cross the Euphrates. He fought at least 16 campaigns and had them carved on the walls of Karnak. His great-grandson Amenhotep the Third inherited the profits. He ruled for about 38 years, mostly in peace. He married Tiye, a courtier's daughter, and announced it on large stone scarabs sent around the country, like royal press releases. Other scarabs boast that he shot 102 lions in his first 10 years. He built Luxor Temple's great colonnade, a vast palace across the river, and the mortuary temple whose two giant statues we call the Colossi of Memnon. Late in life he called himself the dazzling sun disc, and his son took that idea much further. Look at any scarab in a shop or museum: a sun, a beetle and a game board spell Menkheperre, Thutmose the Third.
